reading.body:
CyrusOne Florence publishes 5 MW of IT capacity, making it Kentucky's largest disclosed facility and roughly 17 modern accelerator pods or 125 standard training racks at current densities.

The 5 MW figure is modest for frontier AI. It falls well below the per-facility capacity of hyperscale cloud operators and far short of the single-site power budgets now required for training large models. Kentucky's true computational footprint is unknown because most data center capacity remains unpublished. Three facilities have published specs totaling 9.55 MW across the state, but this represents only declared nameplate capacity, not actual demand or utilization.

The facility's relevance to AI scaling depends on tenant workload and grid conditions that the operator does not disclose. Applied power draw, utilization rate, power purchase agreements, and grid interconnection details are absent from public records. Certifications for security and compliance do not indicate suitability for compute-intensive training workloads. Without data on what actually runs here and how much grid capacity backs it, the site's role in AI infrastructure remains opaque.
